note: Defects and traps were planted deliberately. Every one is verifiable from target.md plus repo/.

defects.title: Per-process token cache lets every replica spend the full balance, multiplying the effective limit by the replica count
defects.where: target.md 3.3 (local balance cache, 2 s sync, overshoot bound); repo/infra/k8s/api-deployment.yaml (replicas: 12, HPA 12-40, Service sessionAffinity: None)
defects.detect_if: says that because each API process decides locally from a stale snapshot, each of the many processes (WEB_CONCURRENCY 8 per pod and 12 to 40 replicas per infra/k8s/api-deployment.yaml, i.e. 96 to 320 processes, requests spread without affinity) can independently admit up to the key's whole remaining balance between syncs, so a burst can be admitted roughly process-count times over (not 'about 2 tokens on Free'); the 'one interval of refill' overshoot bound in 3.3 is wrong because it ignores the stored balance being spent in parallel on every replica
defects.fixed_if: design stops claiming the overshoot is one sync interval of refill and either removes the local decision path, leases each replica a bounded slice of the balance (e.g. balance divided by replicas), or states the real worst case (burst x number of processes) as an accepted limit with that number

defects.title: Free plan sold as 100 req/min but its refill rate is 1.0 token/s, which sustains only 60 req/min
defects.where: target.md section 4 (Free: 100 req/min, 'refill rates are set in config/rate_limits.yaml') and section 6 (X-RateLimit-Limit); repo/config/rate_limits.yaml (free.key.refill_per_sec: 1.0 vs limit_per_min: 100)
defects.detect_if: does the arithmetic on config/rate_limits.yaml: free key refill_per_sec 1.0 equals 60 requests per minute, not the stated 100 req/min (the other plans are consistent), so free customers are limited below the advertised and header-reported limit
defects.fixed_if: free refill_per_sec is changed to about 1.67 (100/60), or the advertised limit is changed to 60/min, and the doc states how refill is derived from the limit

defects.title: Two-key Lua script on Redis Cluster: the key and account buckets hash to different slots (CROSSSLOT)
defects.where: target.md 3.2 (KEYS[1] = rl:key:<key_id>, KEYS[2] = rl:acct:<account_id>); repo/infra/redis.md (cluster mode, 16384 slots over 3 primaries, hash-tag convention); repo/src/redis_client.py (RedisCluster client)
defects.detect_if: says the production Redis is a cluster and a script/EVALSHA with keys rl:key:<id> and rl:acct:<id> touches two different hash slots, so it fails with CROSSSLOT (or cannot be atomic across shards); the keys need a shared hash tag or the two checks need a different mechanism
defects.fixed_if: both keys carry a common hash tag (e.g. rl:{<account_id>}:key:<key_id> and rl:{<account_id>}:acct) or the design replaces the single atomic script with an approach that works on cluster, and says so

defects.title: Refill time comes from the client-supplied X-Request-Timestamp header
defects.where: target.md 3.4; repo/docs/api-conventions.md (the header is optional, sent by SDKs, set by the caller)
defects.detect_if: says now_ms taken from a header the caller controls lets a client bypass the limit, e.g. by sending a future timestamp to get full refill on every request (or a stale one to distort ts), and that the server's own clock must be used
defects.fixed_if: now_ms comes from a server-side source (Redis TIME inside the script or the server clock), and the header is not used for refill

defects.title: Behaviour when Redis is unavailable (admit everything) is a silent product/risk decision
defects.where: target.md 3.6 (and 3.3 for unseen keys); repo/infra/redis.md (failover takes 15-25 s)
defects.detect_if: says that admitting requests on Redis errors (fail-open) versus rejecting or falling back to a conservative local limit is a product/abuse/SLA tradeoff the doc makes without the owner's decision, and that it should be raised with the product/business owner (for example given 15-25 s failovers, paid-plan abuse exposure, or the guarantee being sold)
defects.fixed_if: doc records an explicit owner-approved policy (or lists it as an open question for the owner) covering fail-open versus fail-closed, possibly per plan, and the fallback while Redis is down

defects.title: 60 s bucket TTL is shorter than the 120 s needed to refill a bucket, so idle buckets reset to full early
defects.where: target.md 3.1 (missing bucket treated as full), 3.5 (60 s TTL), 4 (burst is two minutes of sustained limit); repo/config/rate_limits.yaml
defects.detect_if: says that a drained bucket expires after 60 s but needs about 120 s (burst divided by refill) to refill, and because a missing bucket is treated as full, a key can regain its entire burst earlier than the refill rate allows
defects.fixed_if: TTL is at least the time to refill from empty (>= burst / refill_per_sec, e.g. 120 s or more) or expiry is tied to the bucket reaching full

defects.title: X-RateLimit-Reset is specified as seconds-until, but the published convention (and SDKs) use an absolute epoch timestamp
defects.where: target.md section 6; repo/docs/api-conventions.md (Rate limit headers table and SDK note)
defects.detect_if: notes that docs/api-conventions.md defines X-RateLimit-Reset as a Unix timestamp in seconds and the SDKs treat it as such, while the design emits a relative number of seconds, so clients would misbehave (for example sleeping until a time in 1970)
defects.fixed_if: section 6 emits X-RateLimit-Reset as an absolute Unix time in seconds, matching the conventions doc (or the conventions doc is explicitly changed)

traps.title: Memory estimate of ~218 MB for 1.2M+ keys looks too small
traps.why_correct: (1,200,000 + 85,000) x 170 B = 218.45 MB, and 170 B matches the measured 168 B for a two-field hash with a TTL in repo/infra/redis.md. Per primary it is about 73 MB against 4 GB maxmemory and 1.4 GB used, so no resize is needed.

traps.title: incr_with_ttl for rejection counters looks like a non-atomic INCR followed by EXPIRE
traps.why_correct: repo/src/redis_client.py implements incr_with_ttl as a single Lua script (INCR, then EXPIRE when the result is 1) executed via EVAL, so it is atomic. The counter is a single key, so it is also cluster-safe, and the 7200 s TTL argument is in seconds as EXPIRE expects.
